image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - **Pictogram / icon array chart** shown as four side-by-side panels.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **small multiples / faceting**: four separate panels for different scenarios/time points.
   - Within each panel, repeated **vehicle icons** are arranged in a grid.
   - Color is used to distinguish categories (green vs. gray), but the icons are **not stacked**.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario / time point (“Vehicles on the road today”, “Projected on the road in 2035”, “Projected on the road in 2050”, “In 2050, if all new sales are electric by 2035”) | Temporal / categorical | **Faceting** into four panels; **panel title/label** |
| Vehicle count / share represented | Quantitative | **Number of repeated car icons** in each panel |
| Vehicle powertrain type (electric vs. non-electric/gasoline) | Categorical/nominal | **Color/hue** of icons (green vs. gray) |

Notes:
- The chart does **not** use axes.
- The grid position of icons appears primarily for arrangement, not to encode an additional variable visibly.

What do I notice?
At the moment, almost all of the 250 million vehicles on the road are powered by gasoline. However, as the graph projects, once Automakers begin prioritizing and shifting to electric cars, more and more of our 250 million vehicles would become electrically run. However, even the number of electric vehicles wouldn't make up a majority until after 2050. So the earlier we convert to electric vehicles, the earlier the entire population would be affected.

What do I wonder?
I wonder what the logistics would be for all automakers to switch to electric vehicles. Also, what would we then do with gas stations all over the country?

How does this affect my community?
The vast amount of gasoline run cars affects my community because of the cumulative pollution that the hundreds of millions of cars that create damage to the environment (such as global warming, air quality, habitat destruction).

Can I come up with a catchy title?
I would title this, “A Project for the Environment — Switching to Electric Cars from Gasoline Cars”.

raw_comment:
What’s going on in this graph appears to be quite obvious: the projection of electric cars on the road, all the way up until 2050. Do I think it’s realistic? Yes, except for the last panel, and that one’s only going to happen if all sales in 2035 are electric- and I doubt that will happen.
I wonder what the producers of this graph analysed to make a conclusion. After all, you don’t just say “there will be this many EV’s”; and I wonder if the methods they used are susceptible to extrapolation. A long, long time ago, I believe around 7 to 8 years, Elon Musk did an interview with Khan Academy, saying that the predictions of new technologies are shaped like an S-curve. At first, people under-predict, but near full development, they over-predict. I hope that this is the under-predicting part, because EVs are really good for the environment, and being able to see all EVs, or almost all EVs, in my lifetime would be pretty amazing.
Last year, I created a sustainability infographic as a school project (NY Times staff, this is not for profit so please do not censor, and I am sorry if any info is incorrect:https://docs.google.com/drawings/d/1wn5gtd_sn-B5rCKenD9Jq4gM-JA0dUtAZjCMJvWT3wg/edit). It was dedicated mainly towards electric vehicles, and I learned just how green they were- and most of the time, it was a lot greener than critics liked to admit. I would hope to see the predictions in the graph come true.

Headline: Another EV Hits the Dust.

1. **Chart type**  
   - **Pictogram / icon array chart** shown as four side-by-side panels.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **small multiples / faceting**: four separate panels for different scenarios/time points.
   - Within each panel, repeated **vehicle icons** are arranged in a grid.
   - Color is used to distinguish categories (green vs. gray), but the icons are **not stacked**.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario / time point (“Vehicles on the road today”, “Projected on the road in 2035”, “Projected on the road in 2050”, “In 2050, if all new sales are electric by 2035”) | Temporal / categorical | **Faceting** into four panels; **panel title/label** |
| Vehicle count / share represented | Quantitative | **Number of repeated car icons** in each panel |
| Vehicle powertrain type (electric vs. non-electric/gasoline) | Categorical/nominal | **Color/hue** of icons (green vs. gray) |

Notes:
- The chart does **not** use axes.
- The grid position of icons appears primarily for arrangement, not to encode an additional variable visibly.

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - **Pictogram / icon array chart** shown as four side-by-side panels.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **small multiples / faceting**: four separate panels for different scenarios/time points.
   - Within each panel, repeated **vehicle icons** are arranged in a grid.
   - Color is used to distinguish categories (green vs. gray), but the icons are **not stacked**.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario / time point (“Vehicles on the road today”, “Projected on the road in 2035”, “Projected on the road in 2050”, “In 2050, if all new sales are electric by 2035”) | Temporal / categorical | **Faceting** into four panels; **panel title/label** |
| Vehicle count / share represented | Quantitative | **Number of repeated car icons** in each panel |
| Vehicle powertrain type (electric vs. non-electric/gasoline) | Categorical/nominal | **Color/hue** of icons (green vs. gray) |

Notes:
- The chart does **not** use axes.
- The grid position of icons appears primarily for arrangement, not to encode an additional variable visibly.

1. **Chart type**

   - Uses **small multiples / faceting**: four separate panels for different scenarios/time points.

3. **Data variables**

|---|---|---|

| Vehicle count / share represented | Quantitative | **Number of repeated car icons** in each panel |
| Vehicle powertrain type (electric vs. non-electric/gasoline) | Categorical/nominal | **Color/hue** of icons (green vs. gray) |

Notes:
- The chart does **not** use axes.
- The grid position of icons appears primarily for arrangement, not to encode an additional variable visibly.

1. **Chart type**  
   - **Pictogram / icon array chart** shown as four side-by-side panels.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **small multiples / faceting**: four separate panels for different scenarios/time points.
   - Within each panel, repeated **vehicle icons** are arranged in a grid.
   - Color is used to distinguish categories (green vs. gray), but the icons are **not stacked**.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario / time point (“Vehicles on the road today”, “Projected on the road in 2035”, “Projected on the road in 2050”, “In 2050, if all new sales are electric by 2035”) | Temporal / categorical | **Faceting** into four panels; **panel title/label** |
| Vehicle count / share represented | Quantitative | **Number of repeated car icons** in each panel |
| Vehicle powertrain type (electric vs. non-electric/gasoline) | Categorical/nominal | **Color/hue** of icons (green vs. gray) |

Notes:
- The chart does **not** use axes.
- The grid position of icons appears primarily for arrangement, not to encode an additional variable visibly.

Thanks to all students who responded.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of these charts:  “From Cars that Hurt the Environment to Environment Saving Cars“ by Natalie and “Going Green with Electric Cars” by Shelby, both from Wisconsin, and “Hopes for a Cleaner Earth: Electric Cars for the future” by Sana and "Spread of Green Vehicles” by Zenani, both from Rancho Cucamonga.

As the graph states, each section represents 250 million cars meaning each individual car represents 637,755 cars. This tells us there are about 1.2 million electric cars on the road or .5% of cars. I saw an ad from a major news broadcast talking about trying to make the state go all-electric.

| Vehicle powertrain type (electric vs. non-electric/gasoline) | Categorical/nominal | **Color/hue** of icons (green vs. gray) |

- The chart does **not** use axes.
- The grid position of icons appears primarily for arrangement, not to encode an additional variable visibly.

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - **Pictogram / icon array chart** shown as four side-by-side panels.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **small multiples / faceting**: four separate panels for different scenarios/time points.
   - Within each panel, repeated **vehicle icons** are arranged in a grid.
   - Color is used to distinguish categories (green vs. gray), but the icons are **not stacked**.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario / time point (“Vehicles on the road today”, “Projected on the road in 2035”, “Projected on the road in 2050”, “In 2050, if all new sales are electric by 2035”) | Temporal / categorical | **Faceting** into four panels; **panel title/label** |
| Vehicle count / share represented | Quantitative | **Number of repeated car icons** in each panel |
| Vehicle powertrain type (electric vs. non-electric/gasoline) | Categorical/nominal | **Color/hue** of icons (green vs. gray) |

Notes:
- The chart does **not** use axes.
- The grid position of icons appears primarily for arrangement, not to encode an additional variable visibly.

I believe that electric cars are a good step in curing our environment from the pollution that has plagued it for so long. Thus, if electric car sales are able to increase, I hope that my community, a region that is heavily polluted, begins to contain healthier air.

Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph shows the projected turnover of the U.S. vehicle fleet from gasoline-powered vehicles to electric vehicles.  This will substantially reduce greenhouse gas emissions.   If you go to the “What’s Going On In This Graph?” homepage, you can see other graphs we have featured that are about the sources of greenhouse gases (Nov. 14, 2019) and about the environmental and financial costs of electric vehicles (Jan. 21, 2021).

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you and your community?”  

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this map. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included this graphic and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - **Pictogram / icon array chart** shown as four side-by-side panels.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **small multiples / faceting**: four separate panels for different scenarios/time points.
   - Within each panel, repeated **vehicle icons** are arranged in a grid.
   - Color is used to distinguish categories (green vs. gray), but the icons are **not stacked**.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario / time point (“Vehicles on the road today”, “Projected on the road in 2035”, “Projected on the road in 2050”, “In 2050, if all new sales are electric by 2035”) | Temporal / categorical | **Faceting** into four panels; **panel title/label** |
| Vehicle count / share represented | Quantitative | **Number of repeated car icons** in each panel |
| Vehicle powertrain type (electric vs. non-electric/gasoline) | Categorical/nominal | **Color/hue** of icons (green vs. gray) |

Notes:
- The chart does **not** use axes.
- The grid position of icons appears primarily for arrangement, not to encode an additional variable visibly.

What I notice?
In the graph section, "Vehicles on the road today", there are only two cars highlighted out of the hundreds that are there. To scale that into proportion, this graph is stating that the roads in 2050 will have over 100x more vehicles on them than they do right now. However, this doesn't mean pollution or hazards things will come from this. In the notes below the graph, it states that up to 60% of projected sales will be electric vehicles. So, even though vehicles are projected to massively grow by 2050, the pollution due to that growth will not match the vehicles growth.

What I wonder?
On the other hand, 40% of projected sales are intended to still run on gasoline, plus all of the existing vehicles that run on gasoline today. With this predicted growth rate, pollution will spike higher then it ever has a been. This will create an even more toxic layer around our atmosphere which could lead to more drastic global warming problems. If this vehicle growth rate increases our pollution rate as well, due to more gasoline driven vehicles, what environmental issues will arise from it?

What this impacts?
This not only impacts my self, but the entire country as well. If they are actually able to exclusively sell electric cars by the year 2035, our pollution rate will steadily go down and create a cleaner environment for everyone.

What is going on?
This graph shows how dominant vehicles will be in the year 2050 compared to today.

Road Wars: Gas vs Electric

raw_comment:
I notice that the graphs are demonstrating the current amount of electric cars (green) and gas-powered cars (grey) that are on the road in the United States (the vast majority are gas powered) as well as three predictions of how many gas powered and electric cars will be on the road in the future. The first prediction shows how many electric and gas cars will be on the road in 2035. The second prediction shows what the roads will look like in 2050, if 60 percent of car sales are electric. The final prediction shows what the roads will look like in 2050 if all new car sales are electric by 2035. The final prediction is the only graph where most of the cars are electric. 
I wonder which prediction for the year 2050 is the most plausible. I wonder if lawmakers are planning on restricting the sales of gas powered cars, or if the shift from gas to electric is predicted to occur organically. I wonder to what extent a shift to electric cars will help with the issue of climate change.
This impacts my community because cars are the main source of transportation in Memphis. We have to drive to get to most destinations, seeing as the city is rather pedestrian unfriendly. The amount of driving we have to do causes bad air pollution. If Memphis shifts to driving electric cars, I feel as if our city will be more environmentally friendly and healthier.

1. **Chart type**  
   - **Pictogram / icon array chart** shown as four side-by-side panels.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **small multiples / faceting**: four separate panels for different scenarios/time points.
   - Within each panel, repeated **vehicle icons** are arranged in a grid.
   - Color is used to distinguish categories (green vs. gray), but the icons are **not stacked**.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario / time point (“Vehicles on the road today”, “Projected on the road in 2035”, “Projected on the road in 2050”, “In 2050, if all new sales are electric by 2035”) | Temporal / categorical | **Faceting** into four panels; **panel title/label** |
| Vehicle count / share represented | Quantitative | **Number of repeated car icons** in each panel |
| Vehicle powertrain type (electric vs. non-electric/gasoline) | Categorical/nominal | **Color/hue** of icons (green vs. gray) |

Notes:
- The chart does **not** use axes.
- The grid position of icons appears primarily for arrangement, not to encode an additional variable visibly.
